Under that guess, testing half the objects is a good split. "No light" would mean both nexioms are among the other three, which leaves 3 pairs. "Light" leaves 12 pairs. The result should also start to show me how the machine actually behaves.

The machine lit up, but I still don't know its rule. If it lights when any nexiom is present, at least one of zebile, dopaban or daforor is a nexiom, which leaves 12 possible pairs. If it needs both nexioms, both are in that group (3 pairs). If it needs exactly one, there is one in each group (9 pairs).

Next I'll mix one object from the first group with one from the second. If the machine lights when any nexiom is present, this splits the 12 pairs into 7 (lit) and 5 (dark). It also gives a useful cross-check for the other possible rules.

Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Test 1 lit, so the machine cannot be one that needs both nexioms present. That rule would put both nexioms in {zebile, dopaban, daforor}, and then test 2 could only have lit if the pair were zebile and semoval, which contradicts test 1.

I'll work with the simplest remaining rule: the machine lights when at least one nexiom is present. Under that rule, at least one nexiom is in {zebile, dopaban, daforor} and at least one is in {zebile, semoval}. That leaves 7 possible pairs:
- zebile with dopaban, daforor, semoval, saneki or mubades
- semoval with dopaban
- semoval with daforor

Two yes/no tests give only 4 outcomes, so I can't guarantee separating all 7 pairs. The best I can do is split them as evenly as possible.

Testing dopaban and saneki does that. "Lit" leaves 3 pairs: zebile with dopaban, semoval with dopaban, or zebile with saneki. "Dark" leaves 4 pairs: zebile with daforor, zebile with semoval, zebile with mubades, or semoval with daforor.

TEST: dopaban, saneki
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

If the machine lights when at least one nexiom is present, only three pairs fit all three tests: zebile with dopaban, semoval with dopaban, or zebile with saneki.

I also checked the rule "lights only when exactly one nexiom is present." Under that rule, only zebile with saneki or semoval with dopaban fit.

One test can split three pairs no better than one against two. Testing saneki alone gives that split under either rule:
- **Lit:** the pair is zebile and saneki.
- **Dark:** the pair is dopaban with either zebile or semoval. I won't be able to tell which, so I'll have to choose between those two.

TEST: saneki
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

Saneki alone did not light, so saneki is not a nexiom. That leaves two pairs: **dopaban with zebile**, or **dopaban with semoval**. My tests could not tell these apart for certain, so this is my best choice rather than a sure answer.

- **If the machine lights only when exactly one nexiom is present:** only dopaban with semoval fits. Zebile with dopaban would have put both nexioms on the first test, and the machine would have stayed dark.

I'm choosing dopaban and semoval because that pair fits all four results under either rule.

One last question. If only dopaban were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

**Yes, it would light up.** This follows directly from my test results, whichever rule the machine uses.

- **Saneki is not a nexiom.** Suppose it were, with saneki alone staying dark. Then the dopaban and saneki test would only light if dopaban were the other nexiom. - **Dopaban alone gives the same result as the third test.** Since saneki is not a nexiom, it never affects the machine. Dopaban alone is therefore equivalent to the dopaban and saneki test, which lit.
